blocks.content: DNS load balancing and application LBs both work at layers you control your infrastructure, your servers, your config. Anycast routing works one level deeper, at the network routing layer itself. The internet's own routing protocol becomes the load balancer.

Anycast: the same IP address is announced from multiple physical locations simultaneously. The internet routes each packet to whichever location is topologically closest automatically, with no DNS, no application logic, no proxy.
To understand Anycast, you need to know where it sits among the four ways packets are addressed on a network.

Anycast improves latency, availability, and global scaling.
Anycast is built on BGP (Border Gateway Protocol) the protocol that routers across the internet use to share routing information.
Every major router on the internet knows how to reach every IP block because BGP tells it the path.
With Anycast, you take one IP block (say 1.1.1.0/24) and announce it from multiple physical locations simultaneously via BGP.
Every router in the world sees multiple paths to the same IP and picks the shortest one measured in BGP hops, which roughly correlates to physical distance.

blocks.alt: The same IP announced from three PoPs lets BGP route each user to whichever is fewest hops away

blocks.content: he same IP (1.1.1.1) is announced from multiple locations (Mumbai, London, Singapore).
Each location is called a PoP (Point of Presence).
When a user sends a request, the internet routing system (BGP) chooses the closest path (fewest hops), not a specific server manually.

["Mumbai user → 2 hops to Mumbai PoP → gets routed there
","London user → 1 hop to London PoP → gets routed there
"]
items: Mumbai user → 2 hops to Mumbai PoP → gets routed there
London user → 1 hop to London PoP → gets routed there

blocks.content: Even though the IP is the same, users reach different physical servers based on network proximity.
This is Anycast's most powerful property. If a PoP goes down, BGP stops announcing that IP from that location.
Every router on the internet automatically reroutes to the next closest PoP in seconds, with no DNS change, no LB config update, no human intervention.

blocks.alt: Under normal operation, Mumbai users reach the healthy Mumbai PoP in about 2ms

blocks.content: Mumbai PoP announces IP (1.1.1.1) via BGP. Routers choose the shortest path (2 hops), so Mumbai users hit Mumbai PoP (~2 ms).

blocks.alt: Once Mumbai stops announcing the route, BGP reroutes globally to Singapore within seconds

blocks.content: Mumbai PoP stops announcing the IP. BGP removes (withdraws) that route globally. Routers automatically pick the next best path: Singapore (12 hops) instead of Mumbai.
No TTL, no manual switching. Failover happens automatically via BGP within ~5–30 seconds.

blocks.alt: Spreading a terabit-scale attack across hundreds of PoPs keeps any single one from being overwhelmed

blocks.content: Anycast is why Cloudflare can absorb terabit-scale DDoS attacks.
An attack targeting 1.1.1.1 gets distributed across hundreds of PoPs simultaneously no single PoP gets the full volume. Each PoP absorbs its local share.

blocks.content: Both route users to nearby servers but they work at completely different layers and have very different properties.

blocks.alt: DNS load balancing decides at name resolution and is bound by TTL, anycast decides at the network layer with no TTL at all
A BGP reroute mid-connection breaks a stateful TCP session since the new PoP has no record of it

blocks.content: The TCP session problem: if a user moves (or BGP reroutes mid-connection), their TCP packets start arriving at a different PoP. That PoP has no record of the TCP session connection breaks. This is why Anycast is perfect for stateless protocols (UDP-based DNS, short HTTP requests) but tricky for long-lived TCP sessions.
